title: MongoDB Certified Associate Database Administrator Exam Questions

contents:
Comprehensive list of Free MongoDB Certified Associate Developer exam questions, grouped by official exam domain, curated for cracking the exam with confidence.
Disclaimer: MongoDB is a protected Brand. These exam questions are neither endorsed by nor affiliated with MongoDB, Inc. These are not the official MongoDB Associate Developer exam questions/dumps. These questions are created from the official MongoDB Documentation and the official MongoDB Node.js Driver Documentation. These questions cover all the domains/objectives of the MongoDB Associate Developer official exam, and once you go through these questions and their concepts, you are more than ready to crack the exam in first attempt.
Free Online Practice Exam Take all 55 questions as a timed online practice exam, free:-
Free MongoDB Certified Associate Developer Online Practice Exam
Overview This is an Associate-level certification for developers who use MongoDB with their applications — validating the knowledge and hands-on skill needed to use the database effectively in day-to-day application development. No formal prerequisites. MongoDB recommends candidates have software engineering experience (in any programming language) and have successfully completed MongoDB training, or have equivalent hands-on experience using MongoDB as the backing database for an application. Costs 150 USD per attempt. Candidates who complete the recommended Learning Path get 50% off, and students/educators can qualify for a free exam through MongoDB’s Student and Educator programs. 53 questions (Multiple Choice — one correct response — and Multiple Response — two or three correct responses, with a prompt in the question when multiple selections are required) in 75 minutes, delivered online with proctoring. MongoDB may include a handful of additional unscored questions for statistical purposes; these do not affect your score. Passing score is not publicly published. MongoDB determines the required percentage for each exam through statistical analysis performed by psychometricians, rather than a single fixed, disclosed cut score, and candidates only need to meet the overall required percentage (not a per-domain minimum). The exam is offered in multiple programming languages — the domain on Drivers is presented according to the language selected at registration, though the core CRUD/aggregation/data-modeling questions are language-agnostic. This post uses Node.js driver syntax for the driver-specific questions. MongoDB certifications currently do not expire and are governed by MongoDB’s own product versioning. Associate Developer Exam Study Guide and official exam registration page for more details. 55 Practice Questions # Domain Weight Questions below 1 MongoDB Overview and the Document Model 8% 5 2 CRUD 51% 29 3 Indexes 17% 8 4 Data Modeling 4% 2 5 Tools and Tooling 2% 1 6 Drivers 18% 10 Domain 1: MongoDB Overview and the Document Model (8%) A developer new to MongoDB asks why a MongoDB document can store data types like dates and 128-bit decimal numbers that a plain JSON document cannot. What is the underlying reason? ⬜ MongoDB stores data records as BSON, a binary representation of JSON documents that supports more data types than JSON
⬜ MongoDB stores documents as plain UTF-8 text files parsed by a custom application-layer parser
⬜ MongoDB converts every document to XML internally before writing it to disk
⬜ MongoDB only supports the same data types as JSON, and dates are actually stored as strings
An application needs to record the exact date and time a support ticket was created, so the value can be displayed to users and sorted chronologically in application code. Which BSON type should the developer use for this field? ⬜ Timestamp
⬜ Date
⬜ Regular Expression
⬜ MinKey
Which of the following are valid BSON data types that a field in a MongoDB document can store? (Select three.) ⬜ Decimal128
⬜ Enum
⬜ ObjectId
⬜ Binary data
A product catalog application stores three documents in the same products collection: a physical book with a pages field, an ebook with a fileSizeMB field, and an audiobook with a durationMinutes field — each document has a different shape. Can these three documents coexist in the same collection? ⬜ No — every document in a collection must have identical fields, just like rows in a relational table
⬜ Only if each shape is stored in its own separate sub-collection
⬜ Yes — MongoDB’s flexible document model allows documents in the same collection to have different fields and data types
⬜ Only if schema validation is explicitly disabled for the entire database
Which of the following statements about the _id field in MongoDB are true? (Select three.) ⬜ The application must always explicitly define a value for the _id field before inserting a document
⬜ Every document in a standard collection is required to have a unique _id field that acts as its primary key
⬜ If an inserted document omits the _id field, the MongoDB driver automatically generates an ObjectId for it
⬜ The value of the _id field is immutable once the document has been inserted
Domain 2: CRUD (51%) A developer runs the following command against an inventory collection: db.inventory.insertOne([“item1”, “item2”]). What is wrong with this command? ⬜ Nothing — insertOne() accepts an array of documents just like insertMany() does
⬜ The command is invalid because a collection cannot be named “inventory”
⬜ The command fails because no _id field was explicitly supplied
⬜ insertOne() expects a single document object as its argument, not an array; inserting multiple documents requires insertMany() with an array of documents
An orders document currently has fields _id, status, customer, and total. A developer runs db.orders.replaceOne({ _id: 501 }, { status: “shipped” }). What happens to the customer and total fields? ⬜ They are removed — replaceOne() replaces the entire matched document with the replacement document, keeping only _id and the fields explicitly given
⬜ They are preserved unchanged, since replaceOne() only touches fields explicitly listed in the replacement document
⬜ They are set to null, but the field names remain in the document
⬜ The operation fails outright because customer and total are missing from the replacement document
A products document is currently { _id: 10, name: “Widget” } — it has no price field. A developer runs db.products.updateOne({ _id: 10 }, { $set: { price: 25 } }). What is the result? ⬜ The operation fails because price did not previously exist on the document
⬜ The document gains a new price field set to 25; the existing name field is left untouched
⬜ The entire document is replaced with only { _id: 10, price: 25 }
⬜ $set can only modify a field that already exists — it never creates new fields
A developer wants to update a restaurant document identified by name, setting its violations and borough fields — but if no document with that name exists yet, a new document should be created from the filter and update instead. Which option accomplishes this? ⬜ Run updateOne() twice — once to check existence, once to update
⬜ Use deleteOne() followed by insertOne() unconditionally
⬜ Pass { upsert: true } as an option to updateOne()
⬜ Upsert behavior happens automatically on every updateOne() call with no option needed
A developer needs to increment the metrics.orders field by 1 on every document in a collection where region equals “west”, in a single call. Which update accomplishes this correctly? ⬜ db.sales.updateOne({ region: “west” }, { $inc: { “metrics.orders”: 1 } })
⬜ db.sales.updateMany({ region: “west” }, { “metrics.orders”: 1 })
⬜ db.sales.updateMany({ region: “west” }, { $set: { “metrics.orders”: 1 } })
⬜ db.sales.updateMany({ region: “west” }, { $inc: { “metrics.orders”: 1 } })
While a developer’s application is running db.accounts.findAndModify({ query: { _id: 42 }, update: { $inc: { balance: -100 } } }), another process is concurrently trying to modify the same document. What guarantee does findAndModify() provide in this situation? ⬜ It atomically finds and updates the single matching document — the find and the modify cannot be interleaved with another operation on that document
⬜ It provides no atomicity guarantee; the developer must implement manual locking around the call
⬜ It queues the concurrent operation and executes both changes in an undefined, non-deterministic order without isolation
⬜ It blocks all reads and writes on the entire collection until the operation finishes
A developer needs to permanently remove every document from a logs collection where level equals “debug”, regardless of how many documents match. Which command is correct? ⬜ db.logs.deleteOne({ level: “debug” })
⬜ db.logs.deleteMany({ level: “debug” })
⬜ db.logs.remove({ level: “debug” }, { justOne: true })
⬜ db.logs.drop({ level: “debug” })
A developer wants to look up a single document in a users collection where the age field is exactly 30. Which filter expression correctly performs this simple equality lookup? ⬜ db.users.findOne({ age: { $exists: 30 } })
⬜ db.users.findOne({ $eq: { age: 30 } })
⬜ db.users.findOne({ age: 30 })
⬜ db.users.findOne({ age: “= 30” })
A document has a field tags: [“red”, “blank”, “green”]. Which query correctly matches this document using an equality constraint that checks whether “red” is one of the elements in the array? ⬜ db.inventory.find({ tags: [“red”] })
⬜ db.inventory.find({ tags: { $size: “red” } })
⬜ db.inventory.find({ “tags.length”: “red” })
⬜ db.inventory.find({ tags: “red” })
A developer needs to find every document in a products collection where price is greater than 50 but less than or equal to 200. Which query operators should be used? ⬜ $gt and $lte
⬜ $in and $nin
⬜ $exists and $type
⬜ $elemMatch and $all
A developer wants to find all movies whose rated field is either “G” or “TV-G”. Which query correctly expresses this? ⬜ db.movies.find({ rated: [“G”, “TV-G”] })
⬜ db.movies.find({ rated: { $in: [“G”, “TV-G”] } })
⬜ db.movies.find({ rated: { $all: [“G”, “TV-G”] } })
⬜ db.movies.find({ rated: { $and: [“G”, “TV-G”] } })
A scores document has results: [82, 85, 88]. A developer needs a query that matches only when at least one element of results is both greater than or equal to 80 AND less than 85 — the same array element must satisfy both conditions. Which operator should be used? ⬜ $or
⬜ $exists
⬜ $elemMatch
⬜ $type
Which of the following are logical query operators in MongoDB that join multiple separate query clauses together? (Select three.) ⬜ $and
⬜ $or
⬜ $not
⬜ $nor
A developer wants the 10 most recently created documents in an events collection, ordered consistently even when multiple documents share the same createdAt timestamp. Which query pattern does MongoDB recommend? ⬜ db.events.find().limit(10).sort({ createdAt: -1 })
⬜ db.events.find().sort({ createdAt: -1 }).limit(10) with no unique tiebreaker field
⬜ db.events.find({ limit: 10 }).sort({ createdAt: -1 })
⬜ db.events.find().sort({ createdAt: -1, _id: 1 }).limit(10)
A developer writes the following projection for a find() query: { name: 1, email: 1, password: 0 }. What is wrong with this projection? ⬜ It illegally mixes inclusion (name, email) and exclusion (password) specifications — a projection cannot contain both, except for the _id field
⬜ Nothing is wrong; MongoDB automatically resolves the conflict by including all three fields
⬜ Projections cannot exclude any field under any circumstances
⬜ Projections are limited to exactly two fields
A developer runs let myCursor = db.users.find({ type: “user” }) and wants every matching document loaded into a single in-memory array to pass to another function. Which method call accomplishes this? ⬜ myCursor.explain()
⬜ myCursor.toArray()
⬜ myCursor.count()
⬜ myCursor.close()
A developer needs an accurate count of the number of documents in an orders collection where status equals “pending”, correct even in the presence of an unclean shutdown or orphaned documents in a sharded cluster. Which method should be used? ⬜ db.orders.find({ status: “pending” }).toArray().length only when length is small
⬜ db.orders.estimatedDocumentCount({ status: “pending” })
⬜ db.orders.countDocuments({ status: “pending” })
⬜ db.orders.getIndexes({ status: “pending” })
A developer needs to enable full-text search on a movies collection’s plot and title fields in Atlas, before any $search queries can be run against them. What must be created first? ⬜ A capped collection
⬜ A read-only Atlas Data API endpoint
⬜ A zone-sharded collection
⬜ A MongoDB Search (Atlas Search) index, defined via the Atlas UI, mongosh, Atlas CLI, Compass, or a supported driver
After creating a MongoDB Search index on a movies collection, a developer wants to run a full-text search query for the word “adventure” as part of an aggregation pipeline. Which aggregation stage should be used, and where does it typically go? ⬜ The $search stage, used as the first stage of the aggregation pipeline
⬜ The $out stage, used as the last stage of the aggregation pipeline
⬜ The $merge stage, used anywhere in the pipeline
⬜ The $unset stage, used as the first stage of the aggregation pipeline
A developer needs to compute, for each distinct year in a movies collection with runtime under 1910, the total and average runtime across all matching movies. Which pair of aggregation stages accomplishes this? ⬜ $project to filter by year, followed by $unwind on runtime
⬜ $match to filter by year, followed by $group with $sum and $avg accumulators on _id: “$year”
⬜ $group first, followed by $match to filter the grouped results by year
⬜ $sort by year, followed by $limit to the first matching document
A developer wants each document in a movies collection to include an array field containing every matching document from a comments collection whose movie_id equals the movie’s _id. Which aggregation stage accomplishes this? ⬜ $merge
⬜ $facet
⬜ $lookup
⬜ $redact
A developer builds an aggregation pipeline that filters and groups a large movies collection by year, and wants to write the final results into a new movies_by_year collection instead of returning them to the application. Which stage should be the last one in the pipeline? ⬜ $match
⬜ $skip
⬜ $count
⬜ $out
A developer needs to insert two new pizza documents, update the price on one existing pizza, and delete one discontinued pizza — all as part of a single, controlled call to the database rather than four separate round trips. Which method is designed for this? ⬜ db.pizzas.bulkWrite([…]) with a mix of insertOne, updateOne, and deleteOne operation documents
⬜ Four separate calls to insertOne(), insertOne(), updateOne(), and deleteOne(), run sequentially
⬜ db.pizzas.aggregate([{ $merge: { into: “pizzas” } }])
⬜ db.pizzas.watch() with a change stream handler that performs each operation
A developer needs an aggregation stage that returns only the title and rated fields (plus a computed field) from each matching movie document, dropping every other field. Which stage is designed for this? ⬜ $facet
⬜ $project
⬜ $bucket
⬜ $sample
A document has sizes: [“S”, “M”, “L”]. A developer runs db.inventory.aggregate([{ $unwind: “$sizes” }]). What does this stage produce? ⬜ One output document where sizes becomes the string “S, M, L”
⬜ One output document where sizes is replaced with the number 3 (the array length)
⬜ Three separate output documents, each identical to the original except sizes is replaced with a single string value: “S”, “M”, and “L” respectively
⬜ No output documents, because $unwind requires a numeric field
An e-commerce application needs to transfer funds between two customer wallet documents in a single logical operation: debit one document and credit another, with a guarantee that either both writes succeed or neither does. What should the developer use, and what does MongoDB’s own guidance say about when this is necessary? ⬜ Two separate, unrelated updateOne() calls with no session, since MongoDB guarantees cross-document atomicity by default
⬜ A capped collection, since capped collections automatically roll back partial writes across documents
⬜ A change stream watching both documents, which automatically retries a failed second write
⬜ A multi-document ACID transaction using a session — but MongoDB’s guidance is that for many use cases, embedding related data in a single document avoids the need for one, since single-document writes are already atomic
A developer wants to insert a single document into the students collection in the school database. Which command should the developer use? ⬜ db.students.insertOne({ name: “Ava”, grade: 10 })
⬜ db.students.insertMany({ name: “Ava”, grade: 10 })
⬜ db.students.insert([{ name: “Ava”, grade: 10 }])
⬜ db.students.save({ name: “Ava”, grade: 10 })
What is the main difference between the $set and $project aggregation stages? ⬜ $set and $project are interchangeable aliases for the exact same aggregation stage
⬜ $set adds new fields or overwrites existing field values while automatically keeping every other field in the document, whereas $project must explicitly specify which fields to include, exclude, or compute
⬜ $set can exclude fields from the output, whereas $project is only able to add new fields
⬜ $project automatically keeps every existing field by default, whereas $set requires every field to be explicitly listed
Which Atlas Search operator groups search results into buckets — such as by string values, numeric ranges, or date ranges — and returns a count for each group? ⬜ $group
⬜ compound
⬜ near
⬜ facet
Domain 3: Indexes (17%) A developer notices that a query filtering on the customerEmail field of a large customers collection is performing a full collection scan. Which type of index would most directly improve this query’s performance? ⬜ A single field index on customerEmail
⬜ A geospatial index on a location field
⬜ A text index on an unrelated description field
⬜ No index will help; only adding more RAM improves this query
A query filters for documents where the tags array field contains the value “sale” — for example db.products.find({ tags: “sale” }) — and this query is currently performing a collection scan. What kind of index would MongoDB automatically create if the developer runs db.products.createIndex({ tags: 1 })? ⬜ A hashed index, since MongoDB always hashes array fields
⬜ A multikey index, since tags holds array values, with a separate index entry created for each element in the array
⬜ A single, unsplit index entry that stores the entire array as one opaque value
⬜ MongoDB would reject the request, since array fields cannot be indexed
A query with no filter conditions sorts results by lastName (ascending) and then firstName (ascending), and is currently performing a collection scan followed by an in-memory sort. Which index would best support this query? ⬜ Two separate single field indexes, one on lastName and one on firstName
⬜ A partial index that only indexes documents where lastName exists
⬜ A compound index: db.users.createIndex({ lastName: 1, firstName: 1 })
⬜ A hashed index on lastName
A developer runs db.orders.getIndexes() on a brand-new collection that has never had a custom index created on it. How many indexes does the result show, and why? ⬜ Zero — collections have no indexes until a developer explicitly creates one
⬜ It depends entirely on how many documents are in the collection
⬜ One per shard the collection is distributed across, regardless of custom indexes
⬜ One — every MongoDB collection automatically has a default index on the _id field
A developer is deciding whether to add several new indexes to a collection that receives a very high volume of writes and comparatively few reads. What trade-off does MongoDB’s documentation say the developer should weigh? ⬜ Indexes make matching queries much more efficient, but MongoDB must also update every relevant index on every write, so indexes add write overhead — a real cost on a write-heavy collection
⬜ Indexes only affect read performance and have absolutely no impact on write operations
⬜ Adding more indexes always improves both read and write performance simultaneously with no downside
⬜ Indexes are free to maintain; only the initial createIndex() call has any performance cost
A developer is about to drop an index that several production queries currently rely on. What does MongoDB’s documentation say happens to those queries afterward, and what does it recommend doing first? ⬜ The queries immediately start returning incorrect or incomplete results
⬜ The queries still return correct results, but likely suffer performance degradation; MongoDB recommends hiding the index first to evaluate the impact before actually dropping it
⬜ Dropping an index automatically and instantly recreates an equivalent index in the background
⬜ Dropping an index has no effect on any query, since MongoDB never actually relies on indexes to answer queries
A developer runs db.orders.find({ status: “shipped” }).explain(“executionStats”) and inspects the winningPlan. Which field, and which specific value, tells the developer the query used a full collection scan rather than an index? ⬜ winningPlan.stage equal to “IXSCAN”
⬜ executionStats.nReturned equal to 0
⬜ winningPlan.stage equal to “COLLSCAN”
⬜ queryPlanner.namespace containing the collection’s name
A developer needs to add an index on a field named zip that is nested inside an embedded address sub-document (e.g., { address: { zip: “02139” } }). Can MongoDB index this nested field directly? ⬜ No — only top-level fields can ever be indexed
⬜ Only if the embedded document is first flattened into a separate collection
⬜ Only if the field is renamed to remove the nesting
⬜ Yes — MongoDB documentation states you can create an index on any field in a document, including embedded fields and fields inside embedded documents, using dotted path notation
Domain 4: Data Modeling (4%) An application models an author document alongside the books that author has written and the reviews readers have left on those books. The application almost always needs an author’s basic info together with a short list of their books on a single page, but reviews are numerous, grow unboundedly, and are only loaded separately on a book’s own detail page. Which modeling approach best fits the author-to-books relationship specifically? ⬜ Embed a bounded list of books directly inside the author document (one-to-many, “author to books” is a documented embedding candidate), while keeping the far larger, unbounded reviews in their own separate collection
⬜ Embed the full, unbounded list of reviews directly inside the author document
⬜ Store every author, book, and review as one single flattened document type in one collection with no distinction between them
⬜ Reference the author from within each book document using a separate authors database with no relationship to the books database
A developer’s application frequently uses $lookup to join an orders collection with a products collection just to display each order’s product name and price alongside order details. MongoDB’s schema design guidance identifies this pattern as an anti-pattern. What is the recommended fix? ⬜ Increase the number of $lookup stages used per query to compensate for slow individual joins
⬜ Embed a small, relevant subset of product fields (like name and price) directly into each order document, so the frequently-needed data can be read in a single query without a $lookup
⬜ Convert the products collection into a capped collection to speed up joins
⬜ Disable indexing on the products collection entirely
Domain 5: Tools and Tooling (2%) A developer wants to quickly experiment with realistic data in a new Atlas cluster without writing their own dataset first, and then browse the loaded collections and their documents directly in the Atlas UI. What should the developer use? ⬜ Manually write and insertMany() several thousand documents by hand before any exploration can begin
⬜ Enable encryption at rest, which automatically populates the cluster with example documents
⬜ Load one of Atlas’s Sample Datasets into the cluster, then browse it using Data Explorer in the Atlas UI
⬜ Create a new Atlas organization, which comes pre-loaded with sample collections in every project
Domain 6: Drivers (18%) A developer building a Node.js application needs to connect to and interact with data stored in MongoDB. What should the application use, and what is the recommended practice for how many client instances to create? ⬜ A raw TCP socket the developer implements from scratch, since MongoDB requires a custom binary protocol implementation per application
⬜ The official MongoDB Node.js driver, but a brand-new MongoClient must be created and connected for every single database operation
⬜ Any general-purpose HTTP client library, since MongoDB communicates exclusively over plain REST endpoints
⬜ The official MongoDB Node.js driver, connecting through a single, reused MongoClient instance for the lifetime of the application rather than creating a new client per request
A developer is given the connection string mongodb+srv://appuser:S3cret@cluster0.abcde.mongodb.net/myapp?retryWrites=true&w=majority. What does the appuser:S3cret@ portion of this URI represent? ⬜ Optional authentication credentials — the username and password the client uses to authenticate against the deployment
⬜ The name of the target database, which must always appear immediately after the protocol
⬜ A required cluster region identifier
⬜ A comment that MongoDB drivers ignore entirely
A Node.js application creates a single MongoClient and uses it to run many concurrent database operations across multiple requests. What does the driver’s connection pool do to support this, and why does it help? ⬜ It opens exactly one connection total for the entire application and queues every operation to run strictly one at a time
⬜ It maintains a cache of open connections that operations borrow and return, reducing application latency and the number of new connections the driver has to create
⬜ It creates and destroys a brand-new TCP connection for every single find() or insertOne() call
⬜ It has no effect on performance; connection pooling is purely a security feature with no latency benefit
Using the Node.js driver, a developer wants to insert a single pizza document and, separately, insert three new pizza documents at once. Which pair of method calls is correct? ⬜ myColl.insertMany(doc) for the single document, and myColl.insertOne([doc1, doc2, doc3]) for the three documents
⬜ myColl.insertOne([doc]) for the single document, and myColl.insertOne([doc1, doc2, doc3]) for the three documents
⬜ myColl.insertOne(doc) for the single document, and myColl.insertMany([doc1, doc2, doc3]) for the three documents
⬜ myColl.insert(doc) for both cases, since insert() automatically detects a single document versus an array
Using the Node.js driver, a developer needs to update the quantity field on a single matching document in an items collection, and separately needs to set a random_review field on every movie rated “G” in a movies collection. Which pair of calls is correct? ⬜ myColl.updateMany(filter, { $set: { quantity: 5 } }) for the single document, and movies.updateOne({ rated: “G” }, { $set: { random_review: “…” } }) for every matching movie
⬜ myColl.updateOne(filter, { quantity: 5 }) for the single document, omitting any update operator
⬜ myColl.replaceOne(filter, { $set: { quantity: 5 } }) for the single document
⬜ myColl.updateOne(filter, { $set: { quantity: 5 } }) for the single document, and movies.updateMany({ rated: “G” }, { $set: { random_review: “…” } }) for every matching movie
Using the Node.js driver, a developer needs to remove a single movie document matching a title, and separately remove every movie document whose title matches a regular expression. Which pair of calls is correct, and how can the developer confirm how many documents were removed? ⬜ movies.deleteOne(query) for the single document and movies.deleteMany(query) for every matching document, checking result.deletedCount on each returned result
⬜ movies.deleteMany(query) for the single document and movies.deleteOne(query) for every matching document
⬜ movies.remove(query, { justOne: true }) for the single document, since deleteOne() does not exist in the Node.js driver
⬜ movies.deleteOne(query).count() to get the number of documents removed
Using the Node.js driver, a developer wants to retrieve every document in a movies collection matching a query and iterate over each one with for await…of, versus retrieving just a single matching document. Which pair of methods and their return types is correct? ⬜ find() returns a single document directly; findOne() returns a Cursor instance
⬜ find() returns a Cursor instance to iterate over multiple matches; findOne() returns a Promise that resolves to a single matching document or null
⬜ Both find() and findOne() always return a plain JavaScript array of every matching document
⬜ find() throws an exception if more than one document matches
A developer needs to run a pipeline in application code that groups, renames, and computes new fields from a movies collection — beyond what a simple filter-and-sort find() query can express. Which driver method should be used, and how does it differ from find()? ⬜ collection.find(pipeline) — find() natively accepts an aggregation pipeline array as its only argument
⬜ collection.count(pipeline) — counting is the only way to run multi-stage data transformations
⬜ collection.aggregate(pipeline) — unlike find(), which can select, sort, limit, and count documents, aggregation can additionally group results, rename fields, compute new fields, and merge data across collections
⬜ There is no dedicated aggregation method; all grouping and computed fields must be done in application code after calling find()
A developer wants every write performed through a particular MongoClient to require acknowledgment from at least two replica set members by default, without having to repeat that option on every individual insertOne() or updateOne() call. Where should this be configured? ⬜ It cannot be configured anywhere except by editing MongoDB’s server configuration file directly
⬜ It must be passed as a separate argument to every single insertOne() and updateOne() call, with no way to set a client-wide default
⬜ Write concern can only be set once per calendar day and then locks for 24 hours
⬜ As a writeConcern option passed when constructing the MongoClient (e.g. { writeConcern: { w: 2 } }), which sets the default for all operations run through that client unless overridden at a lower level
How is BSON converted into JSON (JavaScript objects) when using the MongoDB driver for Node.js? ⬜ The driver automatically serializes and deserializes between BSON and native JavaScript objects, so application code works with plain objects without any manual conversion step
⬜ The application must manually call JSON.parse() on every document returned from a query before it can be used
⬜ A separate, third-party JSON conversion library must be installed and called explicitly for every read and write
⬜ The driver returns every document as a raw JSON string, which the developer must parse before accessing any field
Take all 55 questions as a timed online practice exam, free:- Free MongoDB Certified Associate Developer Online Practice Exam
title: MongoDB Certified Associate Developer Exam Questions

contents:
Comprehensive list of Free Certified Kubernetes Security Specialist (CKS) exam questions, grouped by official exam domain, curated for cracking the exam with confidence.
Disclaimer: Kubernetes and the CNCF Certified Kubernetes Security Specialist program are protected brands. These exam questions are neither endorsed by nor affiliated with the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) or The Linux Foundation. These are not the official CKS exam questions/dumps. These questions are created from the official Kubernetes documentation, the publicly published CKS curriculum, and the official docs of the open-source security tooling it covers. These questions cover all the domains of the CKS official exam, and once you go through these questions and their concepts, you are more than ready to crack the exam in first attempt.
Note: The real CKS exam is 100% hands-on and performance-based — you secure and troubleshoot a live cluster in a terminal, not multiple-choice questions. The questions below are concept-check practice questions, in the same format as our other certification posts, meant to solidify your understanding of every CKS curriculum topic before you practice the actual hands-on labs.
Free Online Practice Exam Take all 50 questions as a timed online practice exam, free:-
Free Certified Kubernetes Security Specialist (CKS) Online Practice Exam
Overview This is a performance-based, hands-on certification covering how to secure container-based applications and Kubernetes clusters during build, deployment, and runtime. You must hold an active or expired Certified Kubernetes Administrator (CKA) certification before you’re eligible to sit the CKS exam. The exam costs 445 USD per attempt and includes one free retake. You’ll work through roughly 15 to 20 performance-based tasks in 120 minutes, switching between multiple live clusters in a proctored terminal environment. Passing score is 67%. The curriculum and exam environment track a recent Kubernetes release (the exam environment currently runs Kubernetes v1.35) and are refreshed quarterly. The certification is valid for 2 years. CKS Curriculum and Official Exam Page for more details. 50 Practice Questions # Domain Weight Questions below 1 Cluster Setup 15% 8 2 Cluster Hardening 15% 7 3 System Hardening 10% 5 4 Minimize Microservice Vulnerabilities 20% 10 5 Supply Chain Security 20% 10 6 Monitoring, Logging and Runtime Security 20% 10 Domain 1: Cluster Setup (15%) Two microservices in the same namespace should only be able to reach each other on their required ports, and neither should be reachable from any other Pod in the cluster by default. What implements this? ⬜ A ResourceQuota scoping the namespace
⬜ NetworkPolicies that default-deny ingress/egress and then explicitly allow only the required Pod-to-Pod traffic
⬜ A Horizontal Pod Autoscaler
⬜ Labels alone, with no NetworkPolicy objects
During cluster setup, which tool is purpose-built to run automated checks of a cluster’s configuration against the CIS Kubernetes Benchmark? ⬜ kubectl top
⬜ kube-bench
⬜ kubeadm upgrade
⬜ etcdctl
kube-bench flags a kubelet running with --authorization-mode=AlwaysAllow. Why is this a finding, and what should it be changed to? ⬜ It isn’t a real finding — AlwaysAllow is the recommended kubelet setting
⬜ AlwaysAllow lets any authenticated request to the kubelet API succeed regardless of permissions; it should be set to Webhook so requests are checked against the cluster’s RBAC rules
⬜ It should be changed to AlwaysDeny, which blocks all kubelet API access entirely
⬜ Authorization mode only affects the API server, not the kubelet, so the finding is a false positive
Which practice most directly reduces the risk exposed by leaving the Kubernetes Dashboard deployed on a cluster? ⬜ Avoid deploying the Dashboard where it isn’t needed, and if it must run, restrict access via RBAC, disable its skip-login option, and expose it only through an authenticated proxy
⬜ Deploy the Dashboard with a wildcard ClusterRoleBinding to cluster-admin so any user can self-service
⬜ Expose the Dashboard on a NodePort reachable from the public internet for convenience
⬜ Disable TLS on the Dashboard to simplify troubleshooting
An administrator is provisioning a new cluster and wants to ensure etcd’s client-to-server and peer-to-peer traffic cannot be read or tampered with on the network. What should be configured? ⬜ Nothing — etcd traffic is encrypted by default with no configuration required
⬜ TLS certificates for both etcd client-server and peer communication
⬜ A NetworkPolicy denying all egress from the etcd Pods
⬜ Running etcd with --insecure-transport for simplicity
A Service is exposed externally through an Ingress resource. Which combination best reflects setting up that Ingress with appropriate security control? ⬜ Terminate TLS at the Ingress with a valid certificate, avoid wildcard/overly broad host rules, and restrict it to only the specific paths and backends it needs to expose
⬜ Leave the Ingress on plain HTTP since TLS can always be added later
⬜ Route all traffic for every hostname to every Service in the cluster by default, to save configuration effort
⬜ Grant the Ingress controller’s ServiceAccount cluster-admin so it can never be blocked by RBAC
A Pod running in a cloud-hosted cluster is compromised. The attacker’s process tries to reach 169.254.169.254 from inside the Pod. What is this address, and how should CKS-aligned setup prevent this from being useful to the attacker? ⬜ It’s the cloud provider’s instance metadata service, which can expose node/IAM credentials; a NetworkPolicy (or metadata-service hardening) should block Pods from reaching it unless explicitly required
⬜ It’s a private DNS resolver that all Pods must reach to function, so it should never be restricted
⬜ It’s a Kubernetes internal Service IP that only the API server itself may reach
⬜ It’s an unused, non-routable address with no security relevance
Before installing kubeadm, kubelet, and kubectl binaries on a new node, what should be verified to ensure the downloaded platform binaries haven’t been tampered with? ⬜ Their checksums/signatures against the official published values before installing them
⬜ Nothing — binaries downloaded over HTTPS are automatically trusted and require no further verification
⬜ Only the file size, since a matching size guarantees an unmodified binary
⬜ The binary’s creation timestamp on disk
Domain 2: Cluster Hardening (15%) On a self-managed node, which kubelet flag should be disabled to prevent unauthenticated requests from being treated as an anonymous user with default (often overly broad) permissions? ⬜ --read-only-port=10255 left enabled
⬜ --anonymous-auth=false
⬜ --kubeconfig unset
⬜ --cgroup-driver=systemd
A team wants to grant a CI/CD ServiceAccount permission to create and delete Deployments, but only within the staging namespace, and nothing else. What is the correct, least-privilege RBAC approach? ⬜ Bind the ServiceAccount to the built-in cluster-admin ClusterRole
⬜ Create a Role in the staging namespace with the needed verbs on deployments, and bind it to the ServiceAccount with a RoleBinding in that namespace
⬜ Create a ClusterRoleBinding granting the permissions cluster-wide
⬜ Add the ServiceAccount to the system:masters group
By default, every Pod gets a ServiceAccount token mounted into it, even if the application inside never calls the Kubernetes API. What is the recommended hardening step for Pods that don’t need API access? ⬜ Leave the default token mounted; unused tokens carry no risk
⬜ Set automountServiceAccountToken: false on the Pod or its ServiceAccount, and avoid relying on the namespace’s default ServiceAccount for workloads that do need one
⬜ Rotate the ServiceAccount token every 5 minutes instead
⬜ Grant the default ServiceAccount cluster-admin so any future need is already covered
Which practice best supports “restrict access to Kubernetes API” as part of cluster hardening, beyond RBAC alone? ⬜ Place the API server behind a network boundary (firewall/security group) that only allows traffic from trusted administrative networks, in addition to RBAC and authentication controls
⬜ Expose the API server on a public load balancer with no IP restrictions, relying on RBAC alone
⬜ Disable TLS on the API server to simplify client configuration
⬜ Grant every authenticated user the view ClusterRole by default so nothing is ever accidentally denied
A cluster is still running a Kubernetes minor version that reached end-of-life and no longer receives security patches. From a hardening standpoint, what is the most important remediation? ⬜ Add more replicas to compensate
⬜ Upgrade the cluster to a supported, patched minor version
⬜ Increase the RBAC scope of the cluster-admin role
⬜ Disable audit logging to reduce noise
A user was mistakenly added to the system:masters group instead of being given a scoped Role. Why is this a serious finding during a cluster hardening review? ⬜ system:masters is a hard-coded superuser identity that bypasses RBAC authorization entirely — it cannot be constrained by any Role or ClusterRole
⬜ It’s a low-severity finding since system:masters only grants read access
⬜ system:masters only affects that one user’s own namespace
⬜ system:masters is simply a naming convention with no special permissions attached
A newly created namespace still uses its auto-generated default ServiceAccount for several Deployments, none of which call the Kubernetes API. What’s the recommended hardening step, beyond disabling auto-mount? ⬜ Create purpose-specific ServiceAccounts per workload that actually needs API access, and treat the default ServiceAccount as something workloads should not casually rely on
⬜ Grant the default ServiceAccount cluster-admin so every workload in the namespace is covered no matter what it later needs
⬜ Delete RBAC entirely for the namespace so there’s nothing to misconfigure
⬜ Rename the default ServiceAccount, which alone resolves the underlying risk
Domain 3: System Hardening (10%) A team wants to reduce the attack surface of the underlying host OS that Kubernetes nodes run on. Which action best supports this goal? ⬜ Run a minimal, purpose-built node OS, remove unnecessary packages and services, and keep only what’s required for the container runtime and kubelet to operate
⬜ Install a full desktop environment on every node for easier troubleshooting
⬜ Grant every node’s root user password to the whole platform team for convenience
⬜ Disable the host firewall so container traffic is never blocked
Which Linux kernel-level mechanism restricts what system calls a container’s process is permitted to make, reducing the impact of a container-breakout attempt? ⬜ A Kubernetes NetworkPolicy
⬜ A seccomp profile
⬜ A LimitRange
⬜ A HorizontalPodAutoscaler
Which kernel hardening mechanism uses named profiles to restrict a container’s access to specific files, network operations, and capabilities on the host, and is applied via a Pod’s securityContext on supported Linux distributions? ⬜ seccomp
⬜ AppArmor
⬜ NetworkPolicy
⬜ PodDisruptionBudget
A node’s instance profile (cloud IAM role) currently grants broad admin-level permissions across the cloud account, though the node only needs to pull from one container registry and write its own logs. What should be done? ⬜ Scope the node’s IAM role down to only the specific permissions it needs (e.g. registry pull, log write), following least privilege
⬜ Leave it as-is — broad IAM roles simplify future changes and should be preferred
⬜ Remove the IAM role entirely so the node has no cloud permissions at all, even ones it needs
⬜ Share that same broad role across every node and every workload identity for consistency
Beyond kernel hardening tools, which additional action reduces a node’s exposure at the network layer, in line with “minimize external access to the network”? ⬜ Close or firewall off unnecessary open ports on the node (including restricting direct SSH access to only what’s required, ideally via a bastion/allow-listed source), rather than leaving the host broadly reachable
⬜ Open every port on every node to the internet so troubleshooting is never blocked
⬜ Disable the kubelet’s TLS entirely to simplify connectivity
⬜ Use the same SSH key across every node and hand it out to the whole engineering org
Domain 4: Minimize Microservice Vulnerabilities (20%) An organization wants every Pod deployed in the prod namespace to be denied if it requests privileged mode, host networking, or runs as root. What is the CKS-aligned way to enforce this cluster-wide? ⬜ Rely on developers manually reviewing each other’s manifests before every deployment
⬜ Apply the restricted Pod Security Standard to the namespace via Pod Security Admission (or an equivalent policy engine like Kyverno/OPA Gatekeeper)
⬜ Add a comment in the README asking teams not to do this
⬜ Set a ResourceQuota limiting the number of Pods in the namespace
A cluster needs a custom policy beyond what the built-in Pod Security Standards cover — for example, rejecting any Pod that doesn’t set a specific label required for cost tracking. What kind of tool is designed for this? ⬜ A LimitRange
⬜ A policy engine such as OPA Gatekeeper or Kyverno, enforcing custom admission-time constraints
⬜ A HorizontalPodAutoscaler
⬜ A PriorityClass
A Pod’s container needs to run as a specific non-root UID and must never be allowed to escalate privileges, even if the image’s Dockerfile specifies USER root. Where should this be enforced? ⬜ In the image’s Dockerfile only, since Kubernetes always trusts the image’s declared user
⬜ In the Pod’s securityContext, setting runAsNonRoot: true, runAsUser, and allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
⬜ In a ConfigMap read by the application at startup
⬜ In an Ingress annotation
A container image runs as non-root and can’t escalate privileges, but it still carries Linux capabilities like NET_RAW and SYS_ADMIN that it never actually uses. What further hardens this container’s securityContext? ⬜ Drop all capabilities by default (capabilities.drop: ["ALL"]) and add back only the specific ones the container genuinely needs
⬜ Leave the full default capability set attached, since running as non-root already removes all risk
⬜ Add every available capability explicitly so nothing is ever unexpectedly denied
⬜ Capabilities can only be managed at the node level, not per-container
Which Kubernetes object is specifically designed to store sensitive values such as passwords or API keys somewhat more safely than a ConfigMap, and should further be protected with encryption at rest and RBAC restrictions? ⬜ A ConfigMap
⬜ A Secret
⬜ A LimitRange
⬜ An Endpoint
To prevent Secret data from being readable in plaintext directly from the etcd data store on disk, what should a cluster administrator configure? ⬜ Nothing — etcd never persists Secret data to disk
⬜ Encryption at rest for the Secrets resource, via an EncryptionConfiguration passed to the API server
⬜ A NetworkPolicy blocking traffic to etcd
⬜ A larger etcd disk volume
A workload runs untrusted, third-party code and the team wants stronger isolation than the default container runtime provides, up to and including isolating the workload’s kernel interface from the host kernel. What CKS-aligned control addresses this? ⬜ A resource limits.cpu setting
⬜ A sandboxed runtime (e.g. gVisor or Kata Containers) selected via a Kubernetes RuntimeClass
⬜ A PodDisruptionBudget
⬜ A HorizontalPodAutoscaler
Two microservices exchange sensitive data over the cluster network. Beyond NetworkPolicy segmentation, the team wants the traffic itself encrypted and both sides mutually authenticated at the connection level. What implements this? ⬜ Mutual TLS (mTLS) between the services, typically provided by a service mesh (e.g. Istio, Linkerd) that automatically encrypts and authenticates Pod-to-Pod traffic
⬜ A ResourceQuota on both namespaces
⬜ A HorizontalPodAutoscaler shared between the two Services
⬜ Renaming both Services to use HTTPS-sounding names
A Pod definition includes hostPID: true and hostNetwork: true. From a security-hardening standpoint, what is the concern, and what should generally be done? ⬜ These settings let the container see host processes and use the host’s network namespace directly, significantly widening what a compromised container can reach; they should be avoided unless there’s a specific, justified need and should be blocked by policy otherwise
⬜ These settings are purely cosmetic and have no security implication
⬜ These settings only affect how the Pod is billed for compute, not its access
⬜ These settings are required on every Pod for the cluster to function
An organization has multiple teams sharing a single cluster and wants strong isolation guarantees between their workloads without provisioning separate physical clusters for each. What CKS-relevant concept addresses this trade-off directly? ⬜ HorizontalPodAutoscaler tuning
⬜ Multi-tenancy isolation techniques (namespaces + RBAC + NetworkPolicy + resource quotas, and where needed, sandboxed runtimes or virtual clusters)
⬜ Increasing the etcd disk size
⬜ Disabling RBAC to simplify cross-team access
Domain 5: Supply Chain Security (20%) A cluster administrator wants to restrict which container registries workloads in a cluster are allowed to pull images from, rejecting any Pod that references an untrusted registry. Which mechanism enforces this at admission time? ⬜ A NetworkPolicy scoped to egress traffic
⬜ An admission controller (e.g. ImagePolicyWebhook or a policy engine like OPA Gatekeeper/Kyverno) that validates the image reference against an allow-list of registries
⬜ A ResourceQuota on the namespace
⬜ A PodDisruptionBudget
Before deploying a set of Kubernetes YAML manifests to a cluster, a security-conscious pipeline should run which type of check to catch insecure configuration before it ever reaches the API server? ⬜ A live penetration test against the running Pods
⬜ Static analysis of the manifests (e.g. with kubesec, kube-score, or conftest/OPA policies) as a pre-deployment pipeline step
⬜ A kubectl get events --watch session after deployment
⬜ Manual review of node /var/log files post-deployment
Which of the following is the most effective way to minimize the vulnerabilities present in a container image before it’s ever deployed? ⬜ Add a readinessProbe to the Pod spec
⬜ Build from a minimal, actively maintained base image, keep it updated, and remove build-time tools/package managers from the final image
⬜ Increase the Pod’s memory limit
⬜ Add more application replicas
A pipeline needs to fail the build automatically if a container image contains any package with a known Critical-severity CVE. What kind of tool should be integrated into the CI pipeline? ⬜ A load testing tool
⬜ A container image vulnerability scanner (e.g. Trivy or Grype) run against the built image
⬜ A DNS resolver
⬜ A log aggregator
An organization wants to guarantee that only images built by their own trusted CI pipeline — and not an image with the same tag pushed by someone else — are ever deployed to production. Which practice most directly supports this? ⬜ Always use the :latest tag so the newest image is automatically used
⬜ Cryptographically sign images at build time and enforce signature verification at admission via a policy controller (e.g. Sigstore/cosign with Kyverno or Gatekeeper)
⬜ Rely on the registry’s search feature to manually eyeball image names before deploying
⬜ Store all images in a public, anonymous-write registry for convenience
A Deployment manifest currently pins its image with a mutable tag (e.g. myapp:v2), which could later be overwritten in the registry to point at different image content. What change makes the reference immutable? ⬜ Pin the image by its content digest (e.g. myapp@sha256:...) instead of, or in addition to, the tag
⬜ Switch to the :latest tag, which is guaranteed never to change
⬜ Remove the image reference from the manifest entirely
⬜ Pin the image by its file size instead
A team currently pulls all images directly from public Docker Hub with no internal scanning step. What change most directly improves their supply-chain posture? ⬜ Mirror or proxy approved images through a private, scanning-enabled registry (e.g. Harbor) so every image is scanned and policy-checked before it’s available for deployment
⬜ Continue pulling directly from public registries, since public images are inherently trustworthy
⬜ Disable image pull authentication so deployments never fail due to registry access issues
⬜ Increase the Deployment’s replica count to reduce reliance on any single image pull
A team wants a machine-readable record of exactly which components, libraries, and versions went into a container image, to support vulnerability tracing later. What artifact should be generated as part of the build? ⬜ A kubectl get events dump
⬜ A Software Bill of Materials (SBOM)
⬜ A HorizontalPodAutoscaler manifest
⬜ An Ingress resource
A team is about to adopt a third-party Helm chart from a public chart repository to deploy a component into production. What should they verify before trusting it, beyond simply reading its values.yaml? ⬜ The chart’s provenance/signature (if published) and the images it references, confirming both come from a trustworthy, verifiable source before installing it
⬜ Nothing further — any chart published publicly can be assumed safe to install as-is
⬜ Only that the chart’s name doesn’t contain any unusual characters
⬜ Only that the chart has a high download count, regardless of its contents
An attacker compromises a CI runner’s credentials and pushes a malicious commit that gets built and deployed automatically, even though every image the pipeline has ever produced passed its vulnerability scan. What supply-chain gap does this expose? ⬜ The build pipeline itself — its credentials, runner integrity, and who can trigger or approve a deployment — is part of the supply chain and must be secured, not just the resulting image
⬜ This scenario is impossible if every produced image passes vulnerability scanning
⬜ Vulnerability scanning after the fact would have prevented this regardless of pipeline security
⬜ Only the final production cluster’s RBAC matters; the CI system is out of scope for supply chain security
Domain 6: Monitoring, Logging and Runtime Security (20%) A security team wants to detect unusual behavior at runtime — for example, a container unexpectedly spawning a shell or writing to a sensitive host path — as it happens, not after the fact in application logs. Which class of tool is purpose-built for this? ⬜ A container image vulnerability scanner
⬜ A runtime behavioral-analytics/threat-detection tool such as Falco
⬜ A HorizontalPodAutoscaler
⬜ A NetworkPolicy
Which Kubernetes-native feature records who did what, to which resource, and when, against the API server — essential for after-the-fact incident investigation? ⬜ kubectl top nodes
⬜ Kubernetes audit logging
⬜ LivenessProbe results
⬜ The Horizontal Pod Autoscaler’s metrics history
The default audit policy logs every request at Metadata level, but the security team wants full request AND response bodies captured specifically for secrets access, without generating that much data for every other resource. What should be configured? ⬜ An audit policy with a specific rule matching secrets resources set to RequestResponse level, while lower-sensitivity resources stay at a lighter level such as Metadata
⬜ Set the entire cluster’s audit level to None so no sensitive data is ever logged
⬜ There is no way to vary audit detail by resource type — it’s all-or-nothing
⬜ Enable RequestResponse for every resource in the cluster regardless of sensitivity
After a container is deployed, a policy states that its filesystem should not be modifiable at runtime, reducing the chance a compromised process can persist malicious changes. Which Pod setting enforces this? ⬜ resources.limits.memory
⬜ securityContext.readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
⬜ restartPolicy: Always
⬜ terminationGracePeriodSeconds
An investigator notices repeated, unexpected kubectl exec sessions into a production Pod outside normal deployment hours, followed by outbound connections to an unfamiliar IP. Which type of detection made both of these observable, and what do they together suggest? ⬜ Runtime behavioral monitoring (e.g. Falco rules on exec events) combined with network/audit visibility surfaced a likely lateral-movement or data-exfiltration attempt, not two unrelated events
⬜ Both events are routine and require no further investigation
⬜ Only application logs could have shown this, since Kubernetes has no way to observe exec sessions
⬜ This pattern can only be detected after the cluster is fully rebuilt
During incident response, a compromised Pod is discovered. What should generally happen before the Pod is deleted or the node is rebooted? ⬜ Preserve evidence — capture logs, a process/memory snapshot if possible, and relevant audit trail — so the incident can be properly investigated, rather than destroying state that the investigation needs
⬜ Immediately delete the Pod and move on, since evidence preservation isn’t relevant in Kubernetes environments
⬜ Immediately reboot the node to “clean” it before anyone looks at it
⬜ Grant the compromised Pod additional permissions so it can be observed more easily
A team wants Kubernetes audit logs correlated with node-level and application logs in a central system, so a security analyst can investigate an incident across all three sources at once. What supports this? ⬜ Configure an audit backend (e.g. webhook) to forward audit events to a central log aggregation/SIEM system alongside node and application logs
⬜ Keep audit logs only on the API server’s local disk with no forwarding, since correlation isn’t possible in Kubernetes
⬜ Disable node and application logging so only audit logs need to be reviewed
⬜ Manually copy log files between systems once a year
A Pod was deployed from an image that passed vulnerability scanning and has readOnlyRootFilesystem: true, yet a runtime tool alerts that a new, unexpected binary appeared inside one of its writable volume mounts. What does this most likely indicate, and what kind of control caught it? ⬜ Runtime integrity/behavioral monitoring caught a likely compromise or drift from the container’s expected, immutable state — exactly the kind of detection that build-time scanning alone cannot provide
⬜ This is expected behavior and requires no investigation, since read-only root filesystem guarantees full immutability everywhere in the Pod
⬜ It means the vulnerability scan must have been run incorrectly and should simply be re-run
⬜ Writable volume mounts cannot be monitored at runtime, so this alert should be ignored
A platform team wants to proactively verify, before granting access, exactly what a given ServiceAccount is authorized to do against the API — as a preventive check rather than waiting to detect misuse after the fact. Which command/approach supports this? ⬜ kubectl auth can-i --as=system:serviceaccount:<ns>:<sa> <verb> <resource> to check authorization before an incident, distinct from runtime detection tools that catch misuse after it happens
⬜ Reviewing Falco alerts only, since that is the only way to know what a ServiceAccount can do
⬜ Waiting for an audit log entry showing misuse, since permissions can’t be checked in advance
⬜ Assuming every ServiceAccount has the same permissions as cluster-admin
Which statement best captures why “detect threats within physical infrastructure, apps, networks, data, users, and workloads” is framed as a single, cross-cutting competency rather than several separate ones? ⬜ Real incidents rarely stay confined to one layer — an attacker can pivot through infrastructure, network, or identity weaknesses just as easily as an application bug, so effective detection has to span every layer together
⬜ It means only application-level logging is necessary, since Kubernetes secures the rest automatically
⬜ It means physical hardware never needs to be considered once workloads are containerized
⬜ It means every alert should be routed only to the application development team
Take all 50 questions as a timed online practice exam, free:- Free Certified Kubernetes Security Specialist (CKS) Online Practice Exam
Related Certification Exams Certified Kubernetes Administrator (CKA) Exam Questions — the required prerequisite certification before you’re eligible to sit the CKS exam. Certified Kubernetes Application Developer (CKAD) Exam Questions
